en: Candrāvalokana, Manuscript No. 7970, with additional readings from GOML 4340 (beginning at folio 46v):
Oṃ Maheśvara uvāca [4340 – Oṃ Maheśvara uvāca].
With the internal object of focus and the gaze directed externally, free from blinking and opening—the gaze free from blinking and opening—this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, concealed in all Tantras. ||1||
When the yogi abides with his gaze fixed internally and his mind-wind dissolved,
looking outward and downward with an unblinking, steady vision, he shall never see anything. This indeed is the Khecarī Mudrā, which occurs through the grace of a well-endowed Guru.
That reality which vibrates, free from the duality of emptiness and non-emptiness, is the state of Śambhu. ||2||
With half-closed eyes, his mind throbbing, his gaze fixed upon the tip of the nose, his mind steady, his eyes fixed upon the tip of the nose—
the moon and sun have both reached dissolution;
his body is motionless, a radiant form, supreme, shining intensely, devoid of all external things, and consisting of pure light.
One attains that state of reality which is the supreme goal; what more need be said here?

In that dissolution situated within the innermost core, when the final internal dissolution is realized, one should understand that even while remaining in dissolution, one is joined with a satisfied Guru.
Behold that consciousness which is the witness of the arising and passing away of all beings, residing within the body as the nectar of solid, full bliss. (4)

If the smile is in one place, the mind in another, the power in another, and the vital breath in another, Śiva is not attained even in hundreds of millions of aeons when ascending to the supreme state. ||5||
O Goddess, as long as the vital breath lives, the mind lives;
as long as the mind is perceived, the vital breath also lives.
When this pair—the vital breath and the mind—reaches dissolution, the mind perishes. (6)
That man shall go to liberation; no other ever does.
In various unions and separations, he [attains] the bliss of the *aravinda* (lotus) and so forth.
He who would remain constantly vigilant regarding the signs of non-seeing—he whose vision is not distracted—therein his mind is fixed;
for the eternal nature of the elements and the senses resides where the vision is.
He is the peace of all beings, his vision having attained dissolution in the object of focus.
Wherever there is steadiness of vision, there indeed is the wind (māruta).
This may occur anywhere; thus, for him, that [steadiness] is considered by the perfected ones (siddhas) to be accomplished.
It has the form of an unbroken circle, abiding both outside and inside.
And it is observed that even on the edge of a razor, one does not see with the eye alone.
Like a jewel that constantly flashes, situated at the tip of the eye;
having seen that Śambhu who brings about attainment, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
The light of the self, the light of the mind—the eye does not see that light.
The light that is both external and internal is called Śiva;
as long as the vital breath (māruta) does not enter the central path,
and as long as the drop (bindu) does not become firm and the vital air (prāṇavāyu) is not awakened.
As long as the lake remains similar to the sky, the state of Non-duality (unmanatva) does not arise. 14.
Even if someone who is devoted to constant practice, firm in devotion to the Guru, and unwavering, should speak everything as mere hypocrisy and false chatter; ||15||
He who does not know the innate (sahaja) proceeds like one trapped in an egg.
The new moon day, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon day are kept secret.
At will, she who is stainless and everywhere served as poison—she who is endowed with love at the outset and is to be honored by the worlds—acts like a Brahmin for the people. (16–17)
They do not know things as they truly are, being arrogant and deceitful through false pride.
The new moon day, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon day are kept secret.
"Kāma is stainless poison; he stands above all.
Matsyendra said:
"O Śaṅkara, it is the new moon day, the first lunar day, and the full moon day."
"How is that perception explained? Explain it all according to reality. [4340] "How is that Lord (Īśvara) addressed? [4340] The Lord said:
"The first lunar day (pratipad) is the opening of the eyes; the new moon (amāvāsyā) is the closing of the eyes. [4340] "The new moon is the closing of the eyes."
They call that [night] the full moon (paurṇamāsī) until half of [the moon's] appearance [is visible].
What is meant by the word "Kāma" for Matsyendra? Or what is expressed by the word "poison"?
What is this whose nature is stainless? Tell me this according to reality. (23) [The Lord is of such a nature.]
The path of practice (pratipad) swallows desire, and the new moon day (amāvāsyā) does likewise;

the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) stabilizes the action, and the path becomes otherwise not so. Having stabilized desire through desire, the objects of sense are [transformed]; from the poison of desire, there is its dissolution.
One should always abandon these two and take refuge in the stainless one. ||25||
Another should renounce everything if he desires his own welfare;
otherwise, there is only death, for the elements have already been consumed.
Having placed the mind within the power (*śakti*), and that power within the center of the mind;
having perceived the mind with the mind, one should meditate upon that supreme state.
— Matsyendra.
What is the bindu said to be, and what is the characteristic of the bindu?
And how does the drop (bindu) arise? Explain this according to reality. ||28||
The Lord.
For the mind alone is the drop (bindu) and the cause of both arising and abiding.
From the mind the drop arises, just as milk has the nature of butter.
Matsyendra.
Pervading from the crest-lock to the tips of the nails, it remains within the moon as pleasure and pain.
How can there be a binding for that which flows through the channels and the openings? [The Lord.

There is no bondage situated in the moon, nor is it in the mind of a single sense-organ. Wherever the middle energy (*madhyamā śakti*) resides, there is bondage. Having known the *suṣumnā* and having pierced it, one should place the vital air (*vāyu*) within that middle [channel].
Having performed this, she should restrain it at the station of the Bindu within the nostril. ||32||
Matsyendra.
Wind is declared to be the *bindu*, as well as the *tattva* and *prakṛti*.
I do not know the six cakras; please be gracious and tell them to me.
The Lord.
The Foundation, the Self-Consecration, the Jewel-Filling, and the third, the Heat.
The unstruck [sound], the pure, and the sixth, the wheel of command. || 34 ||
The support (ādhāra) is said to be the anus, and the svādhiṣṭhāna is situated in the middle;
maṇipūra is in the region of the navel, and anāhata is located in the heart.

The *viśuddha* at the region of the throat and the *ājñācakra* at the head. Having fully understood these six wheels (*ṣaṭcakrāṇi*), one should enter the *dhruvamaṇḍala*. [The *ādhāra* is said to be the anus; the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is located in the genitals; the *maṇipūra* is at the region of the navel; the *anāhata* resides in the heart; the *viśuddha* is at the region of the throat; and the *ājñācakra* is at the head. Having fully understood these six wheels, one should enter the *dhruvamaṇḍala*.]
Having drawn in the breath, one should enter it and likewise direct it upwards.
One should practice in this manner until one becomes identical with the entire universe. || 37 ||
One should practice the wind, the drop, and likewise the wheel, joined with the mind.

(4340) Through a single meditative absorption, yogis attain the nectar. (4340) Just as fire situated within wood does not arise without friction, so too [the nectar does not arise without practice]. (4340)
Indeed, without the yoga of practice, there is no illumination of knowledge at all.
Just as a lamp inside a jar does not illuminate the outside,
when that jar is broken and [the light] has gone out, the radiance of the lamp’s flame shines forth.
The word "pot" is said to denote its own intrinsic nature; indeed, that very word denotes the lamp as well.
Through the word of the Guru, the knowledge of Brahman becomes manifest within that which is both identical to and distinct from it.
(41) Having reached the interior of the ear-cavity and having made the subtle internal spaces their own, those who are devoted to the vehicle of practice cross the ocean of worldly existence. (43)
Matsyendra said:
"By the grace of your feet, I am liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
You alone are my guru, O Lord of the gods; it is not otherwise for me, O Śaṅkara. [4340] "You are my refuge, O Lord of the gods."
Having heard the words of Matsyendra, the Blessed Śiva entered [the body].
"Go, my son, upon the earth; you shall uplift the three worlds.
Thus ends the *Candrāvalokana* composed by Mahendra.
[4340 Thus ends the *Candrāvalokana* composed by Maheśva. Homage to the Guru-Nātha.]
